lowest_questions.l3_anchor: Most services have layered automated tests that run on every PR within agreed time budgets.
Key data is cataloged with owners and quality indicators; most questions can be answered within an hour.
Most repositories define a reproducible environment; agents use the same definition.
PR lifecycle metrics are reported per organization; agent-authored PRs are identified separately, including their post-merge fix rate.
A business case with explicit assumptions exists and is reviewed at least yearly.
A survey runs at least twice a year with good participation; results are shared and acted on.
Agent runs emit telemetry to the central observability stack; dashboards show failures and cost per agent.
Pipelines are code in most repositories; AI-assisted failure analysis is available to all teams.
On-call engineers in most teams use AI for triage and summaries; post-incident reviews record whether AI helped.
A review process covers AI components; SBOMs and build provenance are produced for most builds.
Threat models are required for new AI features and agent workflows and reviewed by security.
Agent permissions are documented and reviewed; agents cannot reach production credentials or push to protected branches.
Most teams use AI to draft or improve work items; acceptance criteria are mandatory before work starts.
Plans or specs are stored in the repository or linked to the issue, and are reviewed by a human before agent implementation.
Work items reference the user problem and success measure; feedback is reviewed before prioritization.
Review guidelines explain what to check in AI output; trust in AI output is part of the developer survey.
Required checks are enforced by rulesets on the protected branches of most repositories, with no bypass for agent identities.
AI review runs automatically on most PRs; teams track useful vs dismissed suggestions.

Role-based curriculum (developer, reviewer, platform, security) with completion tracked; training is required before agent features are enabled; it teaches learning-preserving patterns (ask for explanations, attempt first, then compare) and not only full delegation.
Onboarding includes AI-guided codebase tours and repository instructions; time to first merged PR is tracked; new engineers are checked on code reading and debugging, not only output.
Guidance and examples on context engineering are part of training; teams review their instructions and prompts for quality.

Most active repositories have structured instructions (build, test, conventions, constraints) with an owner; changes go through PR review; files are updated when the codebase changes rather than committed once.
Many engineers regularly use at least one GitHub agent surface ("Agent first"), confirmed by usage metrics.
Agent mode is the default for multi-file refactors and features in most teams; changes are reviewed in the diff before commit.
A published matrix maps task types (for example dependency upgrades, test generation, feature work, production changes) to autonomy levels and required approvals.
A named framework is adopted; AI-related risks are in the risk register with owners and reviews.
Enterprise/organization policies enable only approved features and models; the catalog lists owner, data handling and review date for each tool.
